conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that the claim is well-supported and that exemestane reduces breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk based on high-quality randomized controlled trial data. Thus, it endorses the claim.

report:
**Conclusion: The claim is well-supported.** Exemestane does reduce breast cancer incidence in postmenopausal women at elevated risk, based on strong randomized controlled trial evidence.

**Evidence:**

The key evidence comes from the MAP.3 (Mammary Prevention 3) trial, a large, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 study of 4,560 postmenopausal women at moderately increased risk for breast cancer. Published in the *New England Journal of Medicine*, the trial found that exemestane "significantly reduced invasive breast cancers in postmenopausal women who were at moderately increased risk for breast cancer" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1103507). At a median follow-up of 35 months, invasive breast cancer incidence was 0.19% in the exemestane group versus 0.55% in placebo—a 65% relative risk reduction (https://www.academia.edu/20226880/Exemestane_for_breast_cancer_prevention_in_postmenopausal_women).

This finding was corroborated by the National Cancer Institute's summary and by conference coverage from ASCO 2011, both confirming the 65% reduction and describing it as a major advance for high-risk postmenopausal women (https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/research/exemestane-reduces-risk; https://www.hmpgloballearningnetwork.com/site/frmc/articles/exemestane-reduces-breast-cancer-risk-postmenopausal-women). A critical review in PMC similarly summarized the trial results and called it a "potential critical shift" in prevention strategy, noting "few differences in adverse events" between groups (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3354700/).

**Caveats:** Follow-up in MAP.3 was relatively short (median ~35 months), and effects on breast cancer mortality and long-term safety (e.g., bone health) remain less certain, per subsequent analyses. Overall, however, the core claim—reduced incidence—is robustly supported by high-quality RCT data.
